lessons.title: Types of Nursery Containers: Trays, Pots, Bags
lessons.body:
Nursery containers come in three main types: trays, pots, and bags. Each has specific uses and benefits. Plastic trays are shallow, with multiple cells, often 50 to 200 cells per tray. They are ideal for vegetables like tomatoes, peppers, and onions. Trays save space and make watering easy, but roots can circle if left too long. Use trays for short-term seedlings (3-4 weeks) before transplanting.

Pots are individual containers, usually made of plastic or clay. Common sizes are 8 cm, 10 cm, and 15 cm diameter. Plastic pots are lightweight and cheap; clay pots are heavier but breathable, reducing root rot. Use pots for plants that need more root space, like fruit trees or shrubs. They are reusable if sanitized.

Bags, often called polybags, are black plastic bags with drainage holes. Standard sizes: 15 cm x 20 cm for small seedlings, 20 cm x 30 cm for larger trees. Polybags are cheap and widely used in Africa for tree seedlings like mango, avocado, and eucalyptus. They allow deep root growth but tear easily. Always punch 4-6 holes at the bottom for drainage.

Choose based on plant type, root depth, and duration in nursery. Trays for quick vegetables, pots for medium-term plants, bags for trees. In Africa, many farmers use locally available materials like used plastic bottles or banana leaves as containers, but commercial containers give better results. Always ensure containers have drainage holes to prevent waterlogging, which kills seedlings. Sterilize containers before reuse to avoid diseases.

lessons.title: Choosing the Right Container Size
lessons.body:
Container size directly affects seedling health. Too small, roots become pot-bound; too large, soil stays wet and causes rot. Match container size to plant type and how long it stays in the nursery. For vegetables like cabbage, lettuce, and tomatoes, use trays with cells 3-4 cm wide. These are transplanted after 3-4 weeks. For peppers and eggplants, use cells 5 cm wide, as they need 4-6 weeks.

For medium plants like papaya or passion fruit, use pots 10-15 cm diameter. These stay 2-3 months. For trees like mango, citrus, or eucalyptus, use polybags 20 cm x 30 cm or larger. Trees need 6-12 months in nursery, so deep bags (30 cm) allow taproot growth. A rule: container depth should be at least 1.5 times the expected root depth at transplanting.

In Africa, many farmers use recycled containers. If using plastic bottles, cut to 15 cm depth for vegetables, 25 cm for trees. Tin cans work but heat up in sun and rust; paint them white or wrap with cloth. Banana leaves or woven baskets are traditional but dry out fast; line with plastic if possible. Always ensure drainage: 4-6 holes of 5 mm diameter at bottom.

Never overcrowd seedlings. In trays, one seed per cell. In pots, one seedling per pot. Overcrowding causes competition for light, water, and nutrients, leading to weak stems. If you must use a larger container for a small seedling, water carefullyâless frequent but deep. Test soil moisture by sticking finger 2 cm into soil; water only if dry. Correct size saves water, space, and money.

lessons.title: Sanitizing Containers and Tools
lessons.body:
Dirty containers and tools carry fungi, bacteria, and viruses that kill seedlings. Sanitize before every use, especially when reusing. For plastic trays, pots, and bags, wash with soapy water to remove soil. Then soak in 10% bleach solution (1 part bleach to 9 parts water) for 10 minutes. Rinse thoroughly with clean waterâbleach residue burns roots. For clay pots, scrub with a brush, then soak in bleach solution for 30 minutes because clay is porous.

For tools like trowels, pruning shears, and knives, remove soil and sap with a wire brush. Then wipe with 70% alcohol or dip in bleach solution for 5 minutes. Dry in sun. Sunlight itself kills many pathogensâlay tools and containers on black plastic in full sun for 2-3 hours. This is free and effective.

In Africa, bleach may be expensive. Alternatives: boil water and pour over small tools (not plasticâit melts). Use wood ash: mix ash with water to form paste, scrub containers, then rinse. Ash is alkaline and kills some fungi. Or use hot water and soap, then sun-dry. For polybags, never reuse if they had diseased plantsâburn them.

Sanitize between different batches of seedlings. If you had damping-off (seedlings rot at base), throw away all soil and containers, or sanitize twice. Keep a bucket of bleach solution in the nursery. After using a tool, dip it before moving to next plant. This prevents spreading diseases like bacterial wilt in tomatoes. Clean tools last longer and work better.

lessons.title: Essential Nursery Tools and Equipment
lessons.body:
A basic nursery needs these tools: watering can with fine rose (1-2 litre capacity), hand trowel, hand fork, pruning shears, knife, sieve (2-5 mm mesh), wheelbarrow, buckets, and a shade net. A watering can with a fine rose gives gentle water, not washing seeds away. In Africa, use a 5-litre jerrycan with holes punched in the lid as a cheap watering can.

Hand trowel is for filling pots and transplanting. Hand fork loosens soil. Pruning shears cut roots or stems. Knife for cutting bags or grafting. Sieve removes stones and breaks soil clodsâessential for fine seed. Wheelbarrow moves soil and containers. Buckets for water and mixing. Shade net (50-75% shade) protects seedlings from harsh sun. If too expensive, use palm fronds or grass mats.

Other useful items: a dibber (pointed stick) to make planting holes, a ruler or stick marked in cm to measure depth, and a notebook to record sowing dates. For sterilizing, a metal bucket and a source of heat (fire) to boil water. For large nurseries, a knapsack sprayer for foliar feed or pest control.

Buy tools from local agrovets or markets. Quality matters: a cheap trowel bends. Look for metal head with welded handle. In Africa, many tools are made by local blacksmithsâthey are strong and repairable. Keep tools clean and dry. After use, remove soil, wipe with oil (used engine oil works) to prevent rust. Store in a dry place. A well-equipped nursery with 5-6 tools can produce 1000 seedlings per season.

lessons.title: DIY Container Options from Local Materials
lessons.body:
You don't need to buy containers. Many local materials work well. Used plastic bottles are the most common. Cut off the top, punch 4-6 holes in the bottom, and you have a pot. A 1.5-litre bottle is good for vegetables; 5-litre for small trees. Remove labels and wash. Bottles last one season; they become brittle in sun.

Banana leaves or broad leaves: fold into a cone, fill with soil, and plant. They decompose and can be planted directly, but dry out fast. Use for short-term seedlings like maize or beans. Weave baskets from bamboo or palm fronds. Line with a plastic sheet or old cement bag to hold moisture. These are durable for 2-3 seasons.

Tin cans: remove top and bottom, punch holes. Rust quickly, so paint with oil or wrap with cloth. They heat up in sun, so place in shade. Coconut shells: clean, drill a hole, fill with soil. Good for small seedlings like herbs. Old car tyres: cut into rings, fill with soil. Use for large trees. They are heavy but last years.

Egg cartons: use the bottom half for starting small seeds like lettuce. Transplant after 2 weeks. Old shoes or boots: punch holes, fill with soilâworks in a pinch. Always ensure drainage. In Africa, creativity saves money. But remember: DIY containers may not be sterile. Wash with soap and water, then sun-dry before use. If you had disease, don't reuseâburn or bury. For best results, combine DIY for short-term and commercial bags for trees.

lessons.title: Maintaining and Storing Tools
lessons.body:
Clean tools after every use. Remove soil with a stick or brush. For tools with sap (pruners, knives), wipe with a cloth soaked in kerosene or alcohol. Dry completelyâmoisture causes rust. Once a week, sharpen cutting tools with a file or whetstone. A sharp tool makes clean cuts, reducing plant damage. Oil metal parts with a few drops of used engine oil or cooking oil. This prevents rust and keeps moving parts free.

Store tools in a dry place, off the ground. Hang on a wall or keep in a wooden box. In Africa, a simple rack made of poles under a roof works. Never leave tools in the sunâhandles crack. Never leave in rainârust. For long storage, coat metal with grease and wrap in cloth. Store containers stacked upside down to keep out water and pests. Polybags should be kept in a cool, dark place; sun makes them brittle.

Watering cans: empty after use, dry upside down. Shade nets: roll and store away from rodents. Wheelbarrows: store under cover, axle greased. Buckets: stack, but don't leave water insideâmosquitoes breed. Notebooks: keep in a plastic bag to protect from rain.

Make a tool checklist. After work, count tools and put them away. Repair broken handles with local wood. Replace cracked containers. A well-maintained set of tools lasts 5-10 years. This saves money and ensures you are ready for the next planting season. Teach workers to follow the same routine. Clean tools also prevent disease spread between seedlings.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Containers and Tools for African Seedling Nurseries

This practical reference distils the core operational knowledge from the Containers and Tools module of the Seedling Nursery for Farmers course. It is written for African agribusiness owners who treat seedlings as a commercial product â not a hobby. Every decision about containers, tools, and hygiene has a direct effect on germination rates, transplant survival, labour cost, and ultimately your profit margin per seedling sold or planted.

Across sub-Saharan Africa, nurseries range from a few hundred bags under a shade net to thousands of trays supplying commercial vegetable, fruit, and agroforestry value chains. The principles below apply at every scale, but the business logic sharpens as volumes rise: a 5% loss in a 20,000-seedling batch is 1,000 seedlings â real money. Good containers and clean tools are the cheapest insurance you can buy.

1. Container Types and When to Use Them

Container choice is a business decision first, an agronomic one second. Trays suit high-volume, short-cycle vegetable seedlings (tomato, pepper, kale, cabbage) where uniformity and fast transplanting matter. Pots and bags suit tree seedlings, fruit grafts, and any crop that will stay in the nursery for months. Biodegradable options reduce plastic cost and transplant shock but demand careful moisture management.

Table 1: Container types, typical use, and business trade-offs
Container Typical crops Nursery stay Business trade-off
Multi-cell tray (128â288 cells) Tomato, pepper, onion, cabbage, kale 3â6 weeks Low cost per seedling, high throughput; needs uniform watering and a level bed
Plastic pot Tree seedlings, fruit grafts, ornamentals 2â12 months Reusable over many seasons; higher initial cost, heavier to transport
Polythene bag (tube) Agroforestry, banana, coffee, cocoa, oil palm 3â12 months Cheap and widely available; single-use plastic, must be filled and stacked carefully
Biodegradable (leaf, paper, coco) Vegetables, fast tree species 3â10 weeks Zero plastic waste, planted with the seedling; breaks down unevenly if too dry
DIY local (bamboo, calabash, banana leaf) Local vegetables, community nurseries 3â8 weeks Very low cash cost; labour-intensive, less uniform, harder to mechanise

Sources: FAO, Good Agricultural Practices for Seedling Production; ICRAF/World Agroforestry Centre nursery manuals; AVRDC/WorldVeg vegetable nursery guides.

2. Choosing the Right Container Size

Undersized containers are the most common and most expensive mistake in African nurseries. A seedling that runs out of root space before sale becomes stunted, gets a poor price, and often dies after transplanting â damaging your reputation and repeat business. Oversized containers waste potting mix, water, transport space, and money. Match container volume to the target seedling size at sale, not to the seed size.

Table 2: Recommended container volume by crop and target seedling height
Crop group Target height at sale Minimum volume Notes
Leafy vegetables (kale, spinach, amaranth) 10â15 cm 30â50 ml Trays work well; sell within 4 weeks
Fruiting vegetables (tomato, pepper) 15â25 cm 50â150 ml Avoid root binding before transplant
Fast tree species (Grevillea, Sesbania) 30â50 cm 1â2 L Bags or pots; harden off before sale
Fruit trees (mango, citrus, avocado) 50â100 cm 3â5 L Long nursery stay; premium pricing possible
Banana, plantain suckers 30â60 cm 3â5 L Use perforated bags for drainage

Sources: FAO seedling production guidance; ICRAF tree nursery manuals; WorldVeg (AVRDC) vegetable nursery technical bulletins.

3. Sanitizing Containers and Tools

Damping-off, bacterial wilt, and root rot can wipe out an entire batch â and they travel on dirty trays, reused bags, and uncleaned secateurs. Sanitation is not optional; it is a cost-control measure. A 10-minute bleach soak costs almost nothing compared to losing 5,000 seedlings.

Standard practice: Wash containers with clean water and soap to remove soil and roots. Soak in a 10% bleach solution (1 part household bleach to 9 parts water) for 10â30 minutes, then rinse thoroughly and dry in the sun. For tools, wipe blades with 70% alcohol or a bleach solution between plants when working with disease-prone crops. Never reuse bags or trays from a batch that showed disease symptoms without full disinfection.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Chemical and Hygiene Hazards

Bleach and other disinfectants burn skin and eyes, and their fumes are dangerous in enclosed spaces. Always wear gloves and eye protection, mix in a well-ventilated area, and never mix bleach with ammonia or acids â toxic gas can result. Store all chemicals in clearly labelled containers, out of reach of children and away from seed and food stores. When using pesticides or fungicides on nursery stock, follow the label exactly, observe the pre-harvest interval, and wash hands and tools afterwards. Dispose of used disinfectant and rinse water away from wells, streams, and crop beds.

4. Essential Nursery Tools and Equipment

A basic commercial nursery needs a small, reliable tool kit. Buy quality where it affects hygiene and precision (pruning tools, sprayers), and buy cheap where it does not (buckets, labels).

  • Filling and potting: scoop, hand trowel, potting bench or table, soil sieve.
  • Sowing: seed trays, dibber or pencil, fine watering can with rose head.
  • Maintenance: pruning shears, grafting knife (for fruit nurseries), wheelbarrow, shade net, watering cans or drip lines.
  • Protection: knapsack sprayer, gloves, mask, gumboots, first-aid kit.
  • Record-keeping: waterproof labels, marker, notebook or phone app for batch tracking.

Track tool purchases as capital items in your records. A knapsack sprayer that lasts five seasons costs far less per seedling than a cheap one replaced every season.

5. DIY Container Options from Local Materials

DIY containers cut cash costs but raise labour costs. Use them when plastic is expensive or unavailable, when you are testing a new market, or when producing for a community or school nursery where plastic waste is a concern. Common African options include banana-leaf pots, folded newspaper tubes, bamboo sections, calabash shells, and reused cement or milk bags. Always punch drainage holes â waterlogged roots kill seedlings faster than drought. Test a small batch before committing your whole production to a DIY format, because breakdown rates vary with humidity and soil mix.

6. Maintaining and Storing Tools

Clean tools at the end of every working day. Remove soil, dry metal parts, and apply a thin film of oil to blades and hinges to prevent rust â especially important in humid coastal and forest zones. Store tools hanging or on a rack, off the ground, in a dry store. Sharpen pruning and grafting tools regularly; blunt blades crush stems and open wounds to disease. Keep a simple maintenance log: date, tool, action taken. This protects your investment and makes it obvious when a tool needs replacing.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Match container volume to the target seedling size at sale â not to the seed.
  2. Confirm every container has free drainage before filling.
  3. Disinfect reused trays, pots, and bags with 10% bleach, then rinse and sun-dry.
  4. Wear gloves and eye protection when handling bleach or other chemicals.
  5. Keep a dedicated tool kit: trowel, dibber, shears, watering can, sprayer, labels.
  6. Clean and oil metal tools at the end of each working day; store dry and off the ground.
  7. Label every batch with crop, variety, sowing date, and container type.
  8. Review container and tool costs per seedling each season and adjust before scaling up.

Further Reading (Free Official Sources)

  • FAO â Good Agricultural Practices for Seedling Production
  • FAO â Sustainable Vegetable Production and Nursery Management
  • World Agroforestry (ICRAF/CIFOR) â Raising Tree Seedlings in a Nursery
  • AVRDC/WorldVeg â Vegetable Nursery and Seedling Production Resources
  • CGIAR â Nursery Management and Seedling Quality Research

Prepared for the Rise AFRICA Skills course Seedling Nursery for Farmers, module Containers and Tools. Business-first guidance for African nursery enterprises.

quiz.q: Which container type is best for tree seedlings that stay in the nursery for 6-12 months?
quiz.explanation: Polybags are deep and allow taproot growth for trees over long periods.

quiz.q: What is the recommended bleach concentration for sanitizing containers?
quiz.explanation: A 10% bleach solution (1 part bleach to 9 parts water) kills pathogens without damaging containers.

quiz.q: Which tool is used to remove stones and break soil clods?
quiz.explanation: A sieve with 2-5 mm mesh removes stones and creates fine soil for seeds.

quiz.q: How many drainage holes should a polybag have?
quiz.explanation: 4-6 holes at the bottom prevent waterlogging while retaining enough moisture.

quiz.q: What is a cheap alternative to a watering can with a fine rose?
options: A) A bucket with a spoon
B) A jerrycan with holes punched in the lid
quiz.explanation: A jerrycan with small holes in the lid gives a gentle spray like a fine rose.

quiz.q: Which local material is best for making a DIY container that decomposes and can be planted directly?
quiz.explanation: Banana leaves can be folded into a cone and planted directly, decomposing in soil.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid using tin cans as nursery containers in full sun?
options: B) They heat up and can cook roots
quiz.explanation: Metal cans absorb heat, raising soil temperature and damaging roots.

quiz.q: What is the correct depth for a container for a seedling expected to have roots 20 cm deep at transplanting?
quiz.explanation: Container depth should be at least 1.5 times the expected root depth, so 30 cm.

quiz.q: Which tool is best for making planting holes in soil?
quiz.explanation: A dibber is a pointed stick used to make holes for seeds or seedlings.

quiz.q: How often should you sharpen cutting tools?
quiz.explanation: Weekly sharpening keeps tools effective and reduces plant damage.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of clay pots over plastic pots?
quiz.explanation: Clay is porous, allowing air movement and reducing waterlogging.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a recommended way to sanitize tools?
quiz.explanation: Boiling plastic tools will melt them; use bleach or alcohol instead.

quiz.q: What is the ideal shade percentage for a nursery shade net?
quiz.explanation: 50-75% shade protects seedlings from harsh sun without stopping light completely.

quiz.q: Which container is best for starting lettuce seeds for 2 weeks?
quiz.explanation: Egg cartons are shallow and perfect for short-term small seeds like lettuce.

quiz.q: What should you do with polybags that held diseased plants?
quiz.explanation: Diseased polybags can harbor pathogens; burning prevents spread.

quiz.q: Which tool is used to move soil and containers in a nursery?
quiz.explanation: A wheelbarrow is for transporting heavy materials like soil and pots.

quiz.q: How can you prevent rust on metal tools?
quiz.explanation: A light coat of oil (e.g., used engine oil) protects metal from rust.

quiz.q: What is a dibber?
options: B) A pointed stick for making holes
quiz.explanation: A dibber is a simple tool used to make planting holes in soil.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign that a seedling needs a larger container?
options: A) Roots growing out of drainage holes
quiz.explanation: Roots emerging from holes indicate the plant is pot-bound and needs more space.

quiz.q: What is the best way to store polybags?
options: B) In a cool, dark place
quiz.explanation: Sun makes plastic brittle; cool, dark storage extends their life.

quiz.q: Which local material can be used as a free alternative to bleach for sanitizing?
quiz.explanation: Wood ash mixed with water is alkaline and kills some fungi and bacteria.

quiz.q: How many seeds should you plant per cell in a tray?
quiz.explanation: One seed per cell prevents overcrowding and competition.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a fine rose on a watering can?
options: B) To create a gentle spray
quiz.explanation: A fine rose breaks water into small droplets, preventing seed displacement.

quiz.q: Which tool would you use to cut a polybag?
quiz.explanation: A knife is used to cut bags or other materials in the nursery.

quiz.q: What is the recommended size of a polybag for a mango seedling?
quiz.explanation: Mango trees need deep bags like 20 cm x 30 cm to accommodate their taproot.

quiz.q: How often should you sanitize reusable containers?
quiz.explanation: Sanitizing before each use prevents disease carryover between batches.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a good practice for tool maintenance?
options: B) Storing in a dry place
C) Leaving tools in the rain
quiz.explanation: Leaving tools in rain causes rust and damages handles.

quiz.q: What is a cheap alternative to a shade net?
quiz.explanation: Palm fronds or grass mats can provide shade at low cost.

quiz.q: Which container is best for a passion fruit seedling that will stay 2-3 months?
quiz.explanation: A 10-15 cm pot gives enough root space for 2-3 months of growth.

quiz.q: Why is it important to dry tools after cleaning?
quiz.explanation: Moisture on metal causes rust; drying prevents corrosion.
